subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: list all demands and rank them by urgency and importance [Thinking]
passage:
Come, sit, Rafiq. When I was in my last year, my father fell ill, and as his only son I felt pulled in six directions. I'm Bhupen, and my first thought was to try to do everything. Then my roommate Kishan said, "Write all of it down."

So I did. Hospital visits, my exams, two assignments, cooking, the electricity bill. Beside each one I wrote two things: how urgent, how important. When I looked at it, two items were both urgent and important: my father's hospital appointments and the exam ahead. The rest could wait, be shared, or be dropped.

I told the lecturer I'd hand in the assignments late. I asked a cousin to sort out the bills. It felt awkward, but for the first time my head cleared.

qa.q: Whom did Bhupen tell about the late assignments?
How did Bhupen feel before he wrote the list?
qa.a: Bhupen felt overwhelmed, pulled in six directions and at first tempted to try to do everything.

qa.q: What choice at the list stage kept Bhupen from breaking down, and what else could he have done?
qa.a: Ranking everything by urgency and importance let him say no to the rest; he could also have asked Kishan or the cousin to take a larger share.

qa.q: How does Kishan see Bhupen's situation in the story?
qa.a: Kishan saw a roommate heading for exhaustion and gave a practical nudge to write it down, which shows care.

grounding: A final-year student lists hospital visits, exams, assignments and household tasks, and ranks treatment appointments and the exam as top priorities.

The hospital canteen closed at nine, and Amandeep had forty minutes, a cold samosa and a paper napkin. His mother's treatment had moved to three days a week, his final-year exam was in eleven days, and his phone kept buzzing with the group project.
His cousin Rukmini sat across. "You look like you're trying to do everything."
"I am." He smoothed the napkin and wrote everything: Mum's appointments, the exam, the group project, two assignments, cooking, electricity bill, cousin's wedding function, gym.
"Okay," he muttered. "What breaks if I miss it? Mum's appointments. The exam. Those two first." He drew a box around them. "Assignments I can ask to delay. Cooking, Masi offered. Bill takes five minutes. Wedding and gym..." He crossed both out.
"You're saying no to the wedding?"
"I'm saying no to everything that isn't Mum or the exam, for eleven days."

qa.q: How many days were left until Amandeep's exam?
qa.a: His exam was in eleven days.

qa.q: How was Amandeep feeling as he started the list, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and stretched thin, admitting he was trying to do everything while his phone kept buzzing.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep do with the lower-ranked items?
qa.a: He could email his teachers about the assignments and message the group project team with his limits, so saying no is clear to others.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel hearing him cross out the wedding?
qa.a: Rukmini may be surprised but understanding, seeing that he is protecting his mother's care and the exam.

grounding: Shows a final-year student listing hospital visits, exams, assignments and chores, ranking treatment and the coming exam first and saying no to the rest.

In their Lucknow flat, Ujjwal's whiteboard used to hold physics formulas. Now it held everything else.
Papa had come home from hospital two weeks ago and needed checkups every Tuesday and Friday. The final-year practicals started on the 18th. There was also the college fest committee, a friend's startup idea, groceries, Papa's lunch, and a pile of tuition fees to deposit.
His sister Kashish, home from her office, found him standing in front of the board with a marker. "What's this?"
"Ranking it," he said. "Urgent and important first. Papa's checkups. Practicals. Those can't move." He wrote 1 and 2 beside them. "Groceries, Papa's lunch: important, but you and I can share them." He wrote 3. "Fest committee and the startup: not now." He rubbed them off.
Kashish raised an eyebrow. "You loved the fest."
"I did. Just not this month."

qa.q: On which days did Papa need checkups?
qa.a: Papa needed checkups every Tuesday and Friday.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's 'Just not this month' suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests a mix of sadness and resolve: he misses the fest he loved but feels clear that it has to wait.

qa.q: What else could Ujjwal do to share the load?
qa.a: He could agree set days with Kashish for groceries and Papa's lunch, so the shared tasks don't fall back on him by default.

qa.q: How might Kashish see the ranked board?
qa.a: Kashish may feel surprised he dropped the fest, but also relieved to see his plan and her part in it clearly.

grounding: Shows a final-year student listing hospital visits, exams and household tasks and ranking checkups and practicals as top priorities to say no to the rest.
